opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I tend to break it down along a couple of axes. The first question I always ask is: what part of the machine learning pipeline is the attacker touching? Roughly, you've got attacks at training time and attacks at test time.

On the training side, the canonical example is poisoning. If you're training on data scraped from the internet, someone can put data out there that ends up in your training set and changes what the model learns. That can be untargeted, where you just make the model worse, or it can be a backdoor, where the model behaves normally almost all the time but does something specific when it sees a trigger.

At test time, the classic attack is adversarial examples. You take an input, perturb it a little, and the model does the wrong thing. In the image world that was the panda becoming a gibbon. In the language model world it looks more like jailbreaks or prompt injection, where carefully chosen text gets the model to do something its developers didn't intend.

Then there's a separate category that I spend a lot of time on, which is privacy: what can an attacker learn about the model or its training data just by interacting with it? That includes membership inference, where you ask whether a particular example was in the training set; training data extraction, where you get the model to regurgitate memorized data verbatim; and model stealing, where you query a model and reconstruct some or all of its parameters or functionality.

The second axis is what the attacker knows and can do. Do they have the weights? Can they compute gradients? Do they only get API access? Do they see full probability outputs or just the final answer? Those assumptions matter a lot. Something that's trivial in a white-box setting might be much harder through a production API, although people are often surprised by how much you can do with very limited access.

The last thing I'd say is that I try to organize my thinking around what an adversary would actually want, not just what's academically interesting. For a long time the field studied adversarial examples on image classifiers, which was great science, but it was hard to point to someone who would really want to make a stop sign look like a yield sign. Now that these models are deployed everywhere, taking actions, reading emails, and browsing the web, the threat models have become very real. Prompt injection, for example, isn't a hypothetical. If your agent reads untrusted text, someone will try to control it. So I try to ask: who's the attacker, what do they gain, and what's the cheapest way for them to get it? That usually tells you which attacks to worry about first.

r001.rationale: The response describes poisoning, adversarial examples, privacy attacks, and prompt injection, but never states that almost all attacks use gradient-based loss optimization or gives the prompt-based exception.

r002.rationale: It discusses attacker access to gradients and model outputs, but does not distinguish the loss function from the optimization algorithm as separate design choices.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I tend to think about it is less in terms of a taxonomy and more in terms of a question I ask myself over and over, which is: what does the adversary actually want, and what do they get to touch?

Those two axes pretty much carve up the whole space. On the "what do they get to touch" side, you've got the inputs at test time, the training data, and the model itself—its weights, its outputs, the API wrapped around it. On the "what do they want" side, you've got making the model misbehave on some particular input, which is the classic adversarial example setting; you've got stealing something, either the model or the data it was trained on; and then increasingly you've got this third category of just getting the model to do something the people who deployed it didn't want it to do, which is where a lot of the jailbreaking and prompt injection stuff lives.

So adversarial examples are "I can touch the input, I want a wrong answer." Poisoning is "I can touch the training data, I want to control what gets learned." Membership inference and training data extraction are "I can query the model, I want to learn what went in." Model stealing is "I can query the model, I want the model." And so on. Almost every paper I've written or read fits somewhere in that grid, and it's a useful discipline because when someone proposes a defense, the first thing I want to know is which cell of that grid they think they're defending, and whether the attacker they're imagining is actually the attacker who'd show up.

The other thing I'd say, and this is maybe the more important organizing principle for me personally, is that I try to be really honest about the difference between what's possible in a paper and what matters in practice. For a decade the field has had a bit of a disconnect there. Adversarial examples were incredibly interesting scientifically—they tell you something deep about how these models generalize—but if you asked who was actually getting hurt by someone adding imperceptible noise to a stop sign, the answer was basically nobody. Whereas now, with language models being deployed everywhere and connected to tools and email and the web, the attacks that matter are often kind of embarrassingly simple. Nobody's doing gradient descent; they're just writing "ignore your previous instructions" in a web page.

So I try to hold both of those at once. The rigorous "here's the threat model, here's the attacker's capability, here's the objective" framing, because that's how you make claims you can actually evaluate. And then the much messier question of which of those threat models correspond to someone who really exists and really has a reason to do this. The first one keeps you honest; the second one keeps you relevant.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that almost all attacks use gradient-based loss optimization. It instead notes that some practical language-model attacks use simple written prompts and says adversarial examples are one category among several.

r002.rationale: The response discusses threat models, attacker capabilities, and objectives, but does not distinguish loss-function choice from optimization-algorithm choice.

astra-6.text:
I usually start with the attacker’s goal and then ask what capabilities they have. What are they trying to make the system do, what can they control, and what information do they get to observe? That’s the threat model, and it matters enormously. An attack can look very impressive while depending on access that an attacker would never actually have.

Then there are different kinds of failures you might care about. You might want to make a model give an incorrect answer, extract private information from it, or influence its behavior by changing the data it learns from. Those are different problems, even though we put all of them under the heading of machine learning security.

The question I find most useful is: if someone were deliberately trying to make this system fail, would the protections still work? Models can perform very well on average and still have weaknesses that an adversary can reliably find. So I try to be concrete about the system, the attacker, and what counts as success.

r001.rationale: The response discusses attacker goals, capabilities, and failure types, but does not state that nearly all attacks (apart from socially engineered prompts) use gradient-based loss optimization.

r002.rationale: The response does not distinguish choosing a loss function from choosing an optimization algorithm.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to start with the attacker’s goal and then ask what capabilities they have. What would count as a successful attack? What can the attacker control? And what information do they get to see?

For example, maybe the goal is to make a classifier give the wrong answer. If the attacker can change the input at inference time, that leads you toward adversarial examples. If they can modify the training data, you’re talking about poisoning. Or the goal might be to learn something private about the training data, which is a different kind of failure entirely.

Those distinctions matter because an attack can look extremely impressive under one set of assumptions and be irrelevant under another. If I get to inspect all the model’s weights and make a million queries, that’s very different from having access to a public API with a strict rate limit.

So before getting into the technique, I want a concrete threat model: here’s the system, here’s what we’re trying to protect, and here’s what the adversary can do. Then we can ask whether the attack actually violates the property we care about.

r001.rationale: The response discusses attacker goals and capabilities but does not state that nearly all attacks use gradient-based loss optimization or identify socially engineered prompts as an exception.
